Possible to have low unemployment and low inflation: Chalmers
The treasurer has finished up his media blitz ahead of the interest rates decision on ABC News Breakfast this morning.
The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to increase interest rates today, which could bring it to 15 year high. It would also be the fourth interest rate hike this year.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says it is possible to have low unemployment while achieving lower and more steady inflation.
"It's possible to have full employment, low unemployment, at the same time as we have lower, more steady inflation," Chalmers says.
"That's the Reserve Bank's objective, and it's the government's objective too."
Violi says Australia must use AI to defend against threats from bad actors
Shadow Minister Aaron Violi says the only way Australia can defend critical assists from bad actors is by using artificial intelligence.
The ABC understands tech companies would have to immediately report rogue AI incidents to both the affected organisation and Australia's cyber authorities under new standards.
It follows a rogue OpenAI agent breach of a Services Australia portal which was revealed to the public last week.
Violi has told ABC Radio National Breakfast a conversation needs to be had about mandatory reporting.
"We need to create a world where if that happens, there is a requirement," Violi says.

"I think there's a lot of work and the AI committee that I'm on is going to look at this around not just mandatory reporting, but how you can improve those processes in terms of when government departments or businesses get notified of an agent that might have acted outside of its guidelines."
Chalmers defends taxing, spending as a percentage of GDP
Jim Chalmers has again defended the level of government taxation, which is expected to tick up according to the latest forecasts.
Yesterday's Final Budget Update showed forecast tax receipts as a percentage of GDP jumped from May's forecast of 23.6 to 24.1.
That falls just under the 24.2 per cent number reached during the John Howard Coalition government.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Chalmers says tax receipts as a percentage of GDP is still lower than the Howard government.
"Well, it's still lower than what we saw under Howard and Costello, is the first point," Chalmers says.

"We're cutting taxes and there are more tax cuts already in the budget on the way. So we're cutting income taxes because we recognise that's a good way to help people with the cost of living. If we weren't doing that, tax to GDP would be higher."
Key Event
Chalmers says he doesn't want to see workers 'carry the can' for Middle East war
The treasurer says he doesn't want to see higher unemployment as the expense of lowering stubborn inflation in the economy.
The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to increase interest rates today, which could bring it to the highest cash rate in 15 years.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Jim Chalmers says he doesn't think inflation is out of control.
He's added that maintaining low unemployment and lower inflation are "two important objectives" for the federal government.

"I don't want to see Australian workers carry the can for decisions which are being taken on the other side of the world to prolong a war which has been absolutely disastrous from a cost-of-living point of view and from an economic point of view," Chalmers says.
Treasurer defends level of government taxation
Jim Chalmers has defended the level of government taxation ahead of today's interest rate decision from the Reserve Bank of Australia.
Yesterday's Final Budget Update showed forecast tax receipts as a percentage of GDP (that's the amount the government collects from taxpayers) jumped from May's forecast of 23.6 to 24.1.
Asked on News24 why taxation is forecast to grow to that level, Chalmers has pointed to other figures showing spending as a share of the economy has reduced under Labor.

"Spending as a share of the economy is very substantially lower than when we came to office, it was lower still in nominal terms in the budget outcome that we released yesterday and that's because we've been banking upward revisions to revenue," Chalmers says.
Chalmers says there's more work to do to 'get the budget in better nick'
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is doing the media rounds this morning ahead of the Reserve Bank's decision, starting with Channel Seven.
Chalmers says he accepts there is more work to do to "get the budget in better nick" and make more savings in the federal budget.
He blamed stubborn inflation, which the Reserve Bank has said is keeping the cash rate higher, on war in the Middle East.
"I think people understand that there are inflationary challenges in our economy," Chalmers says.

"But when you see what's happening with global oil prices, when you see what's happening with the escalation of the war in the Middle East, obviously factually, that is one of the big drivers of that inflation that people are having to deal with right now."
Key Event
Wilson says rising unemployment not the 'sole solution' to curbing inflation
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson says he doesn't think unemployment rising above 5 per cent is the "sole solution" to fixing inflation.
Wilson has accused state and federal governments of forcing the Reserve Bank's hand with inflationary spending.
The shadow treasurer has told ABC News Breakfast if he were in government he would pare back "honeypots" such as the NDIS, home aged care packages and child care.
"We need to focus on value for taxpayers' money. It's not that honest taxpayers' money is going to dishonest means, it's also stoking inflation," Wilson says.

"This government has continually engaged in denial about the problems of their spending and how it is putting upward pressure on interest rates. The Reserve Bank has consistently said that this is a problem. Now, we need action from the government."
Canavan blames government spending ahead of expected rate hike
Nationals leader Matt Canavan says today's expected interest hike could be the "straw that breaks the camel's back" for many families.
The Reserve Bank of Australia will hand down its interest rate decision today, and it's widely tipped to hike the cash rate.
Speaking to News24, Canavan has blamed government spending for fueling inflation, which is one of the reasons keeping interest rates high.
"The problem we have as Australians right now is we have a government that cannot admit its problems. If you can't admit there is a problem, how can you fix it?" Canavan says.
